Article Title: In 2006, the primary school on the island of Stromboli was closed due to a lack of students; in 2026, it opened for just one student whose family would otherwise have to break up their lives
Article Text:
An island inside an island

A letter for home

A school for a student

A six-year-old girl living beneath one of Europe's most active volcanoes recently became the only pupil at a school that the Italian media is calling the smallest in Europe and where the bell hadn't rung for the past 20 years. On September 10, 2026, Aysha went off to her first day of school in Ginostra, a tiny hamlet on the side of the Stromboli volcano, with a pink backpack and a cone of sweets in her hands. According to Italian news agency ANSA, she was visibly moved as her parents walked her in to meet her teacher, Laura Mongi, who had come down from the outskirts of Milan.The fishing hamlet of Ginostra is part of the town of Lipari, on the Italian island of Stromboli is so isolated that residents have christened it 'the island within an island.' With no roads connecting it to the rest of the island and access only by boat, the community is often left cut off from the rest of the world.A donkey takes care of the logistics, and water comes in by a tanker. The village once had its own primary school, but it closed decades ago when the population dwindled to around 40 residents. "The town of Lipari is spread across six different islands, Lipari, Vulcano, Stromboli, Panarea, Filicudi and Alicudi, plus the hamlet of Ginostra, which is an island in the island: even though it's on Stromboli, it's connected only by sea," Abbate, who's the town's delegate, told the magazine Vita in February.Abbate told Sicilian daily La Sicilia in January that the family would have been forced to split up. "My husband, who has a small construction company, would have had to stay here; me and the child would have had to move,” she said. “To get to Lipari we had to get up at dawn, take the hydrofoil and come back in the afternoon. But in winter it often happens that we stay stuck because of storm surges, so school attendance wasn’t guaranteed. ”Abbate and Bazine, who were born and raised in Mazara del Vallo in western Sicily and has lived in Ginostra for 16 years, according to Vita. They wrote to the mayor, to the head of the Lipari comprehensive school, Patrizia Muscolino, and to the provincial school office in Messina. “Everything started when we wrote a letter explaining all the hardships we have on the island and how impossible it was to get to the other schools,” Abbate told Open. “I’d already talked about it several times in the years before; I was very determined about this choice.”Lipari’s town government filed the formal request on January 8, and the regional school office for Sicily said yes on January 19, according to the education site Orizzonte Scuola. Italian law normally asks for at least 15 pupils to open a primary class, though exceptions are allowed in places at risk of depopulation.Now local authorities have agreed to reopen it after Aysha's parents warned they would have been forced to leave the island. The six-year-old would have to travel to a school in Lipari, the largest island on the Aeolian archipelago. Her parents, Monica Abbate and Raffa Bazine, say they have no intention to leave and insist their daughter is happy as the sole student.She isn’t planning on going anywhere, though. “It’s a bare-bones life. You don’t have the comforts of the city: we have just one grocery store that’s open all year,” she told Open. “But here you figure out what the real priorities are, and everything gets freer, less driven by consumerism. My daughter is growing up close to nature; here you always get around on foot. I’d never change my life.”"We love this little paradise, the nature, the sea, even the volcano that looms over our homes. We don't want to have to leave," Bazine told Italian news outlet Ansa. "She hangs out with peers who stay here for months at a time, and she's learned a few words of German from the neighbours' children who go on vacation in Ginostra. She's a happy child," the parents said.“Emergencies? We’ve had plenty of them with the floods of recent years,” Abbate told Vita. “And then we’re under an active volcano, so for us it’s always staying on alert. Do I think it’s dangerous? I think there are many more dangers in the city.” On Etna, Sicily’s other famous volcano, skiers kept carving turns in December 2025 even as ash and smoke rose behind the ridge line.The new school will feature a single classroom in a building owned by the local parish of the Catholic Church. "The opening of the school is 'a sign of solidarity for this isolated community'," said Riccardo Gullo, the village's mayor. "Schooling should be 'a fundamental right', even for people living in remote areas," he added.Father Nino Pirrotta, the parish priest, said, "Schools are not just a place of learning; they are a focus for the community."The teacher will follow a customised ministerial program, marking a significant precedent for the protection of the right to education in geographically disadvantaged areas and in combating the depopulation of small Italian towns.Whether the school stays open beyond Aysha’s first year depends on how many pupils enrol in the years ahead, since a full primary cycle requires steady attendance numbers. Families on nearby islands such as Filicudi still face serious schooling gaps, showing that Ginostra’s success has not yet spread across the region. Officials have been clear that the current setup meets one family’s specific need, and broader policy changes for isolated communities remain an open question.
Article Summary: Six-year-old Aysha Abbate is the only pupil at a school on the island of Stromboli. Ginostra, on the side of the volcano, has no roads and access only by boat. The village once had its own primary school, but it closed decades ago when the population dwindled to around 40.

Article Title: Trump faces backlash over plans to import Russian diesel ahead of US midterms
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump.

What is in the Russia diesel deal?

Fuel prices add to Trump's midterm challenge

Trump announces energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine

US President Donald Trump is facing bipartisan criticism over his decision to allow Russian diesel into the US market, as rising fuel prices linked to the Iran war threaten to become a political liability for his Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections.Trump announced on Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by additional shipments in the coming months, to help ease global fuel shortages and bring down prices for American consumers.The move has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties, who argue that easing restrictions on Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with funds to continue its war against Ukraine.The backlash comes just weeks after Trump signed legislation authorising fresh sanctions and tariffs against countries importing Russian oil and gas.A bipartisan group of seven senators on Sunday urged the president to reverse course, saying the US should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russian forces continue to kill Ukrainian civilians.“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine,” the lawmakers said in a joint statement.The group included Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, along with Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.The US Treasury Department is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7 to facilitate the shipments, according to reports. Other Russian assets, including those held in American banks, remain frozen.Trump said Russia would release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another one million tonnes thereafter.He also referred to a further three million tonnes to be delivered within a short period, depending on the condition of Russian refineries damaged in Ukrainian attacks.Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the figures to state-owned news agency Tass, adding that exports could eventually reach three million tonnes per month.“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the arrangement in an interview with Fox News, saying it would operate through existing legal channels available to the administration to help bring down prices. He rejected claims that the agreement would violate US law.Some Republicans have also backed Trump's approach. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer described it as an example of the president thinking outside the box to address the financial pressure on Americans.Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso said the sanctions legislation gave Trump flexibility and additional leverage in dealing with Putin.However, other Republicans have called for tougher action against Moscow. Senator Lisa Murkowski urged Trump to use the new law to increase pressure on Russia rather than allow it to earn additional revenue from diesel exports. Republican Representative Don Bacon also argued that buying Russian fuel was the wrong way to bring down prices.Democrats have been more sharply critical. Representative Steny Hoyer called the deal outrageous, while Representative Bill Keating described it as a disturbing capitulation to Putin. Senator Chris Van Hollen accused Trump of seeking to finance Russia's war against Ukraine after the Iran conflict drove up fuel prices.The dispute comes at a politically sensitive time for Trump, with next month's midterm elections set to determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress.The US-Israel war with Iran, which began at the end of February, has disrupted crude oil supplies and pushed up global energy prices. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for American farmers, ranchers and truckers, who depend on the fuel to operate machinery and transport goods.The average price of diesel in the US stood at $6.28 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association, down from a record $6.53 at the end of September.The rising cost of fuel has added to public dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the economy and the Iran war. Polls indicate that a majority of Americans disapprove of his performance on both issues, putting additional pressure on the administration to demonstrate that it can bring prices down before voters head to the polls.Analysts have questioned whether Russia can deliver the promised volumes and whether the shipments would significantly reduce costs for American consumers. The US consumes approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel per day, meaning the initial 300,000-tonne shipment would account for only a fraction of its daily demand.The deal has also drawn criticism from US allies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a gift to Putin, arguing that the arrangement would provide financial support to Russia while its war against Ukraine continues. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting have also criticised the move, calling for greater pressure on Moscow to end the conflict.Amid the controversy, Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, without providing further details.The proposed arrangement would halt attacks on the two countries' energy infrastructure. Zelensky welcomed the announcement but said Kyiv was awaiting details and confirmation from Moscow.“The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,” Zelensky wrote on X. He added that Ukraine expected Putin to follow through on Trump's announcement.There was no immediate response from Moscow.The energy ceasefire could offer a potential opening for reducing attacks on critical infrastructure, but the diesel arrangement has exposed divisions in Washington over how to balance domestic economic pressures with the US policy of pressuring Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.With fuel prices weighing on voters ahead of the midterms, Trump faces the challenge of delivering relief to American consumers without further alienating lawmakers who believe his Russia policy risks undermining efforts to end the war.
Article Summary: Trump announced on Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel. The move has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties, who argue that easing restrictions on Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with funds to continue its war against Ukraine. The backlash comes just weeks after Trump signed legislation authorising fresh sanctions and tariffs against countries importing Russian oil and gas.

Article Title: A Connecticut town paid $455,000 for a historic two-family home to create about 20 library parking spaces; a state preservation council has now voted to ask the attorney general to stop its demolition
Article Text:
The property, located at 29-31 Eldridge Street, stands next to Manchester's new Main Street library.

House can be restored

Why town wants to demolish?

Concerns over historic district

A plan to demolish a historic house in Manchester, Connecticut, to make space for additional library parking has faced opposition from the state's Historic Preservation Council. The town purchased the two-family property for $455,000 in June 2026, intending to replace it with around 20 parking spaces. However, preservation officials have now voted to seek intervention from the state's attorney general to prevent the demolition, according to CT Insider.The property, located at 29-31 Eldridge Street, stands next to Manchester's new Main Street library. It is part of the Cheney Brothers Historic District, an area recognised as a National Historic Landmark in 1978. The house was originally built to accommodate workers employed at the Cheney Brothers silk mills.The town's decision to demolish the building drew objections from some residents and members of the local historical society. Their concerns ultimately led to a review by Connecticut's Historic Preservation Office.On Wednesday, the Historic Preservation Council unanimously voted to ask the attorney general to intervene under the Connecticut Environmental Protection Act.The law allows action against the 'unreasonable destruction' of protected resources. Although commonly used to protect natural resources, it can also be applied to historic buildings.During the council meeting, preservation advocates argued that the property should be repaired rather than demolished.According to Brad Schide, a member of Preservation Connecticut, restoring the house would be a more appropriate solution. “The structure should be rehabbed and maintained in its present configuration. That to us is the prudent and feasible alternative,” Schide said.Dave Goslin, a principal at Krosky Architects, also assessed the building. Goslin, whose firm handles preservation projects, rated its quality eight out of 10. He said the house had remained in relatively good condition considering its age, although renovations were necessary.“When it was built it was well built and it has held up pretty well over time. The conditions within the building are tired. It’s in need of renovations,” Goslin said.Goslin suggested that Manchester could sell the property to a developer interested in historic preservation. Such a buyer could restore the building and continue using it as a two-family residence.He also proposed another option that would allow the town to create some parking without removing the house. Under this plan, the garage would be demolished to make room for approximately 10 parking spaces. However, Goslin acknowledged that the arrangement would leave the property with a 'substandard' lot and effectively turn its backyard into a parking area.Manchester officials maintained that the house was in poor condition and that keeping it would create additional maintenance costs.Town Manager Steve Stephanou described the property as an eyesore and defended the proposed demolition. “We cannot afford to operate and maintain a structure that frankly has been blighted for some time,” Stephanou said.He added that the building had not been properly maintained over the years and that vehicles had previously been parked on its lawn.According to Stephanou, the new library already has 54 parking spaces included in its plans. The town expects parking demand to increase, and the additional 20 spaces could eventually be reserved for library employees. He also argued that removing the building would eliminate a blind spot at the rear of the parking lot.Preservation advocates raised concerns beyond the future of this particular house. Schide warned that demolishing one historic property could encourage the removal of others in the neighbourhood.“We find it all the time. Buildings, as they are removed, it kind of encourages other removal. If there’s too much of that you lose everything," Schide said.He noted that Eldridge Street still retains much of its historic character and that preserving the house would help protect the wider district.Stephanou responded that Manchester had no intention of demolishing other historic buildings. He said the town would even sign an agreement preventing further removals.However, Andy Horowitz, a Historic Preservation Council member and the state historian, argued that the district's National Historic Landmark designation already provided a basis for protecting its buildings. “It’s hard to argue here unambiguously that it’s beyond repair,” Horowitz said. He maintained that the existing historic designation should be sufficient reason to oppose demolition.
Article Summary: The town purchased the two-family property for $455,000 in June 2026, intending to replace it with around 20 parking spaces. Preservation officials have now voted to seek intervention from the state's attorney general to prevent the demolition. The house was originally built to accommodate workers employed at the Cheney Brothers silk mills.

Article Title: At 76, a retired Australian doctor restored 120 hectares of a 200-hectare property with thousands of native trees, turning a long-term conservation project into a legacy for future generations
Article Text:
Photo credit: Stuart Walmsley/The Guardian

From a farmhouse to a conservation project

She wants the land protected after her lifetime

Photo credit: Stuart Walmsley/The Guardian

Other retirees are spending their later years restoring nature

When Susan Downes bought an old farmhouse in York, Western Australia, she had imagined a quiet life in the countryside, with a small garden to look after. Instead, she found herself the owner of a 200-hectare property, including a hill where old native trees had survived more than a century of grazing but much of the vegetation beneath them had disappeared. Nearly two decades later, the 76-year-old retired general practitioner has turned a substantial part of the land into a conservation project. About 120 hectares have been restored, around 45,000 native seedlings have been planted, and 45 plant species have returned naturally from seeds already present in the soil. As reported by The Guardian, Downes is now working to ensure that the work continues long after she is gone.Downes was in her 60s, widowed and with her children grown up, when she began looking for a home in the countryside. The farmhouse in York appealed to her, but the size of the property initially seemed impractical. A second visit changed her mind. At the back of the farm, she discovered Mount Mackie, a 295-metre hill where ancient York gums and wandoos had survived about 150 years of grazing. Much of the understorey had vanished, leaving the old trees as some of the most visible remnants of the original landscape.“I felt a great connection to the land,” Downes told The Guardian.She decided to buy the property and began looking for ways to restore it. Her first step was to obtain a small local grant to control foxes and feral cats. She then secured funding for 24,000 trees over three years, giving her the means to begin planting on a larger scale. Downes had started her professional career as a botanist, but restoring a large property required more than an interest in plants. The work involved managing invasive animals, removing weeds, planting seedlings and organising the practical details of a long-term conservation effort. Today, the restoration covers 120 hectares of her working farm. The return of 45 plant species through the soil's natural seed bank has also contributed to the recovery of the landscape.For Downes, restoring the land is only part of the task. She also wants to ensure that the area cannot be cleared again in the future. She is working to place the restored land under a conservation covenant, a legal arrangement that can protect land from certain forms of development or clearing. The project is supported by Friends of Mt Mackie, a local volunteer group with a core team of about eight people and more than 80 others who take part in organised planting and seed-collection days. Downes has also been thinking about who will look after the property in the future. The deaths and dementia diagnoses of friends have made her more conscious of how uncertain the time available to complete a long-term project can be.She told The Guardian that she wants the arrangements for the land's future responsibility to be firmly established. Her hope is that her children and grandchildren will be inspired by the work, while the wider community will continue to have access to the place. The project also has a cultural dimension. Ballardong women from York visit Mount Mackie several times a year for cultural healing sessions. Downes is working with Ballardong elders to find an Aboriginal name for the hill. Planning is also under way for a reconciliation event in 2030, marking 200 years since European arrival in the region.Downes is not the only older Australian devoting time to conservation. There are also volunteers and former farmers who have taken on projects ranging from monitoring wildlife to restoring large areas of damaged land, as reported by The Guardian.
Article Summary: Susan Downes bought a 200-hectare property in Western Australia in her 60s. The 76-year-old retired general practitioner has turned a substantial part of the land into a conservation project. About 120 hectares have been restored, around 45,000 native seedlings have been planted.

Article Title: Nick Jonas co-founded a diabetes nonprofit that created 8,400 insulin-access plans in 2025; how its US programme helps people find affordable treatment
Article Text:
Nick Jonas. Images Credit: Wikipedia

Nick Jonas’s insulin-access programme helps people find affordable treatment

Image Credit: Healthcare Radius

The programme builds on Jonas’s personal experience with diabetes

What did Beyond Type 1 achieve with its insulin programme in 2025

The online tool matches users with assistance based on their needs

The quick-start guide explains how people can use the service

Access to affordable insulin remains a challenge for people living with diabetes in the US, particularly those who struggle with insurance coverage or the cost of prescriptions. Singer Nick Jonas , who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at the age of 13, has helped address this problem through Beyond Type 1 , the diabetes nonprofit he co-founded. Its GetInsulin programme connects people with financial assistance and savings options suited to their circumstances. According to the organisation’s 2025 Impact Report, the initiative created 8,400 personalised insulin-access plans during the year, with treatment costing almost always $35 a month or less.Beyond Type 1 introduced GetInsulin in 2020 to help Americans find ways to obtain insulin when its price becomes difficult to manage. As explained in the organisation’s article, Nick Jonas launched an initiative to increase access to affordable insulin. Jonas joined forces with the nonprofit to develop a free online search tool that helps people identify available assistance.The initiative was designed around a practical problem. People who need insulin may find themselves facing high pharmacy bills, uncertain insurance coverage or difficulty identifying programmes that could reduce their expenses.Finding the right option can involve navigating different eligibility rules and application processes.GetInsulin aims to make that search simpler by bringing relevant information together. Instead of requiring users to investigate numerous programmes independently, the website asks for a few details and generates a personalised action plan.The original launch also involved collaboration with the NAACP and Feeding America, according to Beyond Type 1’s 2020 announcement. The initiative reflected an effort to make information about affordable insulin more accessible to people who might otherwise struggle to find support.Jonas’s involvement in diabetes advocacy is closely connected to his own diagnosis. Beyond Type 1’s official profile of the singer states that he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at 13. Alongside his career in music and acting, he has supported causes involving health, education, human rights and young people.Type 1 diabetes requires people to manage their condition with insulin. For those who depend on the medication, being unable to afford a prescription can create an immediate problem.Beyond Type 1’s announcement about the initiative described insulin access as a human rights issue. That approach places affordability at the centre of the discussion, recognising that people should be able to seek treatment without facing financial barriers that put their health at risk.The programme does not remove every obstacle associated with healthcare costs. Instead, it offers a way to identify existing assistance and understand which options may fit an individual's situation.The organisation’s 2025 Impact Report highlights the scale of the programme’s work. During the year, GetInsulin helped generate 8,400 personalised action plans intended to improve access to insulin. Beyond Type 1 reported that the resulting options almost always made insulin available for $35 a month or less.The report also describes a change in how the initiative supports users. Beyond Type 1 introduced a new email journey for GetInsulin and expanded its media support, moving towards ongoing guidance rather than relying solely on one-time assistance.This distinction matters because a person’s financial or insurance circumstances can change. Someone who finds a suitable programme initially may still need information and support to maintain access over time. Continued guidance can help users revisit their options as their needs evolve.The figure of 8,400 represents personalised plans created, rather than a confirmed count of individual prescriptions filled or people who received insulin directly from the nonprofit. The organisation’s reported results demonstrate the reach of its information and referral service while distinguishing that work from the actual supply of medication.The impact report also places the programme within Beyond Type 1’s broader work during 2025, which included expanding its international activities and supporting the diabetes community through education and advocacy.The Get Insulin programme page explains how the service works. Users answer questions about their location, insurance status, income and insulin prescription. The information helps the platform identify options that may be suitable for their circumstances.The service covers people with different insurance arrangements, including those who are uninsured, under-insured or insured but still facing unaffordable costs. It is available in English and Spanish and is intended for people living with diabetes in the US.Beyond Type 1 also separates the service into 2 routes. Urgent Insulin Support is designed for people who have fewer than 7 days of insulin remaining and may be at risk of rationing their supply. It directs users towards possible options offered through insulin manufacturers.Continuing Need Insulin Support is intended for people whose prescribed insulin has become too expensive at the pharmacy. It helps them build a personalised plan for more reliable access throughout the year. The distinction allows people to look for help according to the urgency of their circumstances.Beyond Type 1’s GetInsulin quick-start guide outlines the information users should gather before beginning. This includes their state and ZIP code, insurance arrangements and insulin brand or prescription.Location is important because some US states have limits on insulin co-payments. The guide notes that certain state caps range from $35 to $100 for a 30-day supply. The options available to an individual can depend on where they live and the type of coverage they have.Once users begin the process, they can follow the website’s prompts to build an action plan. Providing an email address and preferred pharmacy is optional, although these details can make it easier to revisit the plan later. Users can also receive a copy by email.There is an important limitation, however. GetInsulin is neither a pharmacy nor an insurance plan. Beyond Type 1 does not dispense or ship insulin through the service, and the website cannot guarantee that every user will qualify for a particular assistance programme. Instead, it connects people with possible sources of savings and support.For anyone struggling to pay for a prescription, the service provides a starting point for exploring available options and reducing the time spent searching for help.
Article Summary: Beyond Type 1 introduced GetInsulin in 2020 to help Americans find ways to obtain insulin when its price becomes difficult to manage. The initiative created 8,400 personalised insulin-access plans during the year, with treatment costing almost always $35 a month or less. The programme builds on Jonas’s personal experience with diabetes.

Article Title: Woman who bought a £10 ring at a London flea market and wore it for decades saw its 26.27-carat diamond sell for £656,750
Article Text:
The "Tenner" Diamond. Sold for £656,750 (Image: Sotheby's)

How a £10 bargain at a West London car boot sale in Isleworth led to an unexpected diamond discovery

Why the ring looked worthless for thirty years and how a local jeweller suspected a genuine diamond

The "Tenner" Diamond (Image: Sotheby's)

What the Gemological Institute of America report revealed about the 26.27 carat cushion cut diamond

How the bidding at the sale pushed the Tenner diamond to £656,750

Image: Canva

What the Tenner diamond teaches collectors about checking old jewellery

Imagine slipping a cheap, grubby cocktail ring onto your finger, wearing it regularly for many long decades, and never suspecting that it hides a fortune. That is precisely what happened to one woman, who paid just ten pounds for a dull-looking ring at a West London car boot sale, which Americans call a flea market. Thirty years later, a local jeweller's glance, a detailed laboratory report and a frenzied London bidding room transformed her bargain into a viral story that made international headlines. This article explains where the ring came from, what experts discovered, and why such a find is possible.In the late 1980s, according to Sotheby's, a woman was browsing a car boot sale in Isleworth, West London, when a box of costume jewellery caught her eye. She was drawn to some bangles, and paid little attention to a cocktail ring holding a single clear stone. Sigee writes that the ring sat in a rusty old setting and looked dull and filthy, nothing special at all. The seller wanted twelve pounds for the whole lot, and the buyer haggled the price down to ten pounds. The bangles and the ring went home with her. The Guardian, reporting through the Press Association, confirms that the ring was bought in the 1980s and that its owner believed it was a decorative costume jewel.For three decades the ring was simply an everyday piece of jewellery. Sotheby's reports that its owner wore it regularly, as anyone might wear a cocktail ring, convinced it could not be worth anything. Only in 2017 did she take it to a local jeweller, who immediately sensed something special. He suspected a genuine diamond but found it too large to measure accurately, so she telephoned Sotheby's. Jessica Wyndham, Sotheby's Head of High Jewelry in Europe, told Sigee that few people imagine they are carrying a stone of such size, adding that "if you've always believed something isn't valuable, there's little reason to question it. " Wyndham also explained that the mount, a blend of silver and gold typical of the late nineteenth century, tarnished over time, leaving it darker and duller than modern settings.Sotheby's sent the piece to the Gemological Institute of America for evaluation, and Sigee reports that the verdict was striking. The cushion-cut diamond weighs 26.27 carats, carries a colour grade of I and earns an impressive clarity grade of very, very slightly included, level two. The Guardian, in its Press Association report, adds that the stone is thought to have been cut in the nineteenth century, although its history and how it arrived at the Sotheby's sale remain unknown. The older cuts were fashioned to display fire, the splitting of light into spectral colours, whereas modern diamonds are cut to maximise brilliance. She said these proportions give a distinctive personality that collectors now find especially appealing. She added that on first seeing the diamond in person, it was clear the stone was special.After the diamond was confirmed as genuine, the story went viral and made international headlines. The Guardian reports that the sale took place in London and that the stone was snapped up for close to twice that figure, at £656,750, a life-changing sum for its owner according to Sigee. Wyndham said, in comments carried by the Press Association, that it was a thrill to bring the hammer down on two much-discussed objects and see that attention turn into strong bidding competition. The second object was a Cartier diamond brooch worn by Margaret Thatcher, which achieved £81,250 against an estimate of £25,000 to £35,000, with proceeds going to the Endeavour Fund, a charity supporting wounded, injured and sick servicemen and women.The story also carries practical lessons. Sotheby's has handled jewels found hidden in old curtains, tucked into chair upholstery and uncovered beneath floorboards in forgotten garages, though she stressed that the Tenner diamond is remarkable for its size, quality and extraordinary circumstances. For anyone inspired to search a relative's jewellery box, she recommended looking for signatures in the mounts or stamps on the pieces themselves, which are the clearest clues to when an item was made, who made it and its level of quality. Sigee adds that every Sotheby's jewellery specialist is a gemologist who can identify the key characteristics of gemstones. The diamond's former owner still attends car boot sales regularly, knowing treasures may hide in unlikely places.
Article Summary: A woman bought a cocktail ring for £10 at a West London car boot sale in the 1980s. She wore it regularly, convinced it could not be worth anything. In 2017 she took it to a local jeweller, who suspected a genuine diamond. The gem was sent to the Gemological Institute of America for evaluation. The cushion-cut diamond weighs 26.27 carats, carries a colour grade of I and earns an impressive clarity grade of very, very slightly included, level two. It was sold at Sotheby's in London for £656,750.

Article Title: An Arkansas family treated the same fence as its property line for nearly six decades; after new neighbours removed fencing and trees, an appeals court upheld $12,000 in treble damages and an order to
Article Text:
The fence became more than just a fence

Tree removal resulted in $12,000 damages

The fence must be rebuilt

A fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties, after a dispute over trees and fencing reached the state Court of Appeals. The ruling in Floyd v. Bowlin-Lemon, reported by Justia, Leagle and Case Law Wire, affirmed the Bowlins’ boundary claim, a $12,000 treble-damages award and an order requiring the neighbouring owners to rebuild the fence. The case involved adjoining properties in Crawford County and centred on a fence line that the Bowlin family had treated as its southern boundary for decades. According to the Arkansas Court of Appeals, Joy Bowlin-Lemon’s family acquired the property in 1967. The family was shown the existing fence lines when it purchased the land and subsequently used those fences as practical boundaries. The property was used for livestock, including cattle and horses, while the family also maintained the land up to the fence by brush hogging and cutting hay.That arrangement remained unchallenged for decades. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property.The court record says portions of the longstanding fence were removed beginning in 2017, with the fence eventually torn down. Trees in the disputed area were also cut down. The Bowlins eventually filed a lawsuit in 2023, alleging trespass and destruction of their fencing and trees. A Crawford County Circuit Court trial followed in October 2024.The central legal question was whether years of treating the fence as the boundary could establish a legally recognised boundary even if the fence did not precisely match the surveyed property line. The appeals court said yes.Under Arkansas law, a boundary by acquiescence can arise when neighbouring landowners tacitly accept a particular line as the dividing boundary for a long period. The court noted that an express agreement is not required, nor does there need to have been an earlier dispute over the property line.In this case, the decades of maintenance and use along the fence, combined with the absence of objections from neighbouring owners, provided sufficient evidence for the lower court’s decision. The court also noted that the southern fence extended roughly 30 to 40 feet beyond the surveyed property line. Despite that discrepancy, the long-established conduct surrounding the fence supported its recognition as the boundary.The dispute also became costly for the Floyds. The circuit court determined that the trees removed from the disputed area were worth $4,000. The Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld that valuation, finding that testimony about the number and type of trees, photographs of the property and evidence of the clearing provided enough support.The court also upheld treble damages, bringing the total award to $12,000. Arkansas law allows treble damages when someone cuts, destroys or removes trees belonging to another person. The appeals court found enough evidence to support the finding that the tree removal was intentional or, at minimum, sufficiently reckless or negligent to trigger the statute. Among the evidence considered was the presence of no-trespassing signs along the fence and Ty Floyd’s admission that he removed trees and portions of the fencing.The lower court also ordered the Floyds to rebuild fencing along the eastern and southern boundaries. The appeals court left that order intact. It noted that Ty Floyd had indicated during the trial that he was willing to rebuild the fence, while his attorney did not object when the Bowlins requested the injunction.That meant the Floyds could not later challenge the fence-rebuilding requirement on appeal. There was, however, one issue the appeals court sent back to the circuit court. The original judgment did not contain a sufficiently precise legal description of the boundary. The appeals court therefore remanded the case for the limited purpose of adding a specific description that would allow the established boundary to be identified directly from the judgment.The decision underscores how decades of conduct can matter in property disputes. A fence may begin as a practical marker, but when generations of adjoining owners consistently treat it as the dividing line, that conduct can ultimately carry legal weight, even when a later survey points somewhere else.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments box below.
Article Summary: Fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property. The Bowlin family had treated the fence line as its southern boundary for decades.

Article Title: UK PM says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote, warns Europe faces same threat
Article Text: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Russia of interfering in Britain's 2016 vote to leave the European Union, warning that countries across Europe face the same threat.In excerpts from an episode of “The Rest Is Politics” podcast released on Sunday, Burnham said he asked his advisers after becoming prime minister in July whether Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.“I've had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said.“These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he added.Burnham's remarks come amid warnings from UK intelligence agencies about the growing threat of Russian interference in Britain's democratic institutions. His comments are believed to mark the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the Brexit vote.Burnham also said he discussed possible links between Russia and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz when the two leaders met in Berlin last week.“You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe,” Burnham said.“There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” he added.In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee found that the British government had failed to fully assess the potential impact of Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts on the EU referendum.
Article Summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Russia of interfering in Britain's 2016 vote to leave the European Union. His comments are believed to mark the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the vote. Article Title: 'Started to sink backwards': 139 migrants, including 15 children, killed as boat capsizes off Djibouti
Article Text:
File photo: A portion of the vessel floats after it capsized while carrying about 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen, (Reuters photo)

At least 139 migrants, including 15 children, have died and 84 remain missing after an overcrowded boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti while carrying more than 300 people towards Yemen, the United Nations migration agency said on Sunday.The boat was carrying 305 people, most of them Ethiopians, when it sank near Guhere, off Djibouti’s eastern coast, in the Gulf of Aden during the night of October 8-9, according to the international organisation for migration (IOM). At least 82 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals.“Survivors told me that the boat started to sink backwards as soon as they got in it,” Alexandre Coissac, IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti, said, describing the incident as a “devastating loss of life”.The agency initially reported 109 deaths and 116 people missing, but revised the toll to 139 dead and 84 missing after more bodies were recovered. The official count may rise further, as some bodies buried by migrants themselves have yet to be verified by authorities, Coissac told the Associated Press.Djiboutian authorities continued search and rescue operations, while IOM teams provided emergency assistance.The agency said it was assisting 64 survivors at a migrant centre in the coastal town of Obock.The crossing from the Horn of Africa to Yemen via the Bab al-Mandeb strait is a popular but dangerous route for migrants seeking jobs and safety in Gulf countries. The narrow waterway separates Djibouti and Yemen, but the journey carries significant risks amid conflict and instability across the region.“Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East,” the IOM said.Coissac said 150 people aboard the boat had previously been turned back from Yemen but had attempted the crossing again.The agency recorded more than 20,000 incoming movements from Ethiopia to Djibouti since September 10. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the sea route to Yemen, while the number attempting the journey rose by 18%, according to the IOM.The latest disaster follows a shipwreck in March 2026 that left nine people dead and 45 missing.IOM director general Amy Pope urged governments and donors to expand support for search and rescue operations and create safer migration routes.“No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives.”
Article Summary: The boat was carrying 305 people, most of them Ethiopians, when it sank. At least 82 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals. The crossing from the Horn of Africa to Yemen via the Bab al-Mandeb strait is a popular but dangerous route for migrants seeking jobs and safety in Gulf countries.

Article Title: Viola Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island; now she and husband Julius Tennon are donating $1.2 million to help local families
Article Text:
PC: Rhode Island Monthly

A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother

From a childhood in poverty to giving back to her Rhode Island roots

What families will be able to access at the new centre

How the new centre will support thousands of Rhode Island residents

For Viola Davis, the place where she grew up remains part of her story, even after a career that has taken her from Rhode Island to Hollywood. The award-winning actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a $1.2 million investment in Central Falls, the Rhode Island community where Davis once lived. The money will fund a new family engagement centre named after her mother, Mary Alice Davis, whose influence Davis has spoken about in explaining the project. Planned as a permanent base for local services, the centre will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center is being developed through the couple’s Davis-Tennon Foundation. Its purpose is to give residents a place to find practical support, whether they need help feeding their families, accessing educational opportunities or preparing for work.For Davis, naming the facility after her mother gives the project a personal connection. She has described the decision as a way of honouring a woman who continued to believe in people through difficult circumstances. The centre, she said, would carry that spirit forward by supporting individuals and creating opportunities for families.As reported by WJAR, the $1.2 million investment was announced on Monday, 20 July 2026. Rather than funding a single short-term initiative, the donation is intended to establish a lasting community resource in Central Falls, a city closely connected to Davis’s childhood.Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island, an experience that forms an important part of her personal history. She went on to build a career in film, television and theatre, becoming one of the most widely recognised actors of her generation. Her professional achievements have included major industry awards, but her latest investment focuses on a community far removed from the entertainment business.Central Falls was part of the environment in which Davis spent her early years. The new centre offers a way for her and Tennon to direct resources towards residents who may face financial pressures and limited access to services.The couple's contribution is being made through their foundation, which has an existing connection to Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry already serves about 3,000 people each month. The new facility is expected to provide a broader base for that work, alongside services aimed at parents, adults seeking new skills and families looking for guidance.Tennon, who is originally from Austin, Texas, has also expressed his commitment to supporting Rhode Island. Although the state is not his birthplace, he and Davis are directing the investment towards a community that holds particular significance for his wife.The planned facility will bring several services together in one location. These include a parent resource centre, a parent university and adult empowerment programmes, giving parents and other residents access to information and opportunities for learning.Food assistance will remain part of the work. The expanded Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry is expected to build on a service that already reaches thousands of people monthly. The centre will also provide workforce development and financial literacy programmes, along with family engagement activities, educational workshops and community events.For people looking for help with more than one issue, having these services in the same place could make it easier to find the right support. Someone visiting for food assistance, for example, may also be able to access parenting resources or information about employment training.The facility will also serve as the permanent administrative headquarters of the Davis-Tennon Foundation. This gives the organisation a local base from which to coordinate its activities and maintain its work in the area.Angelo Garcia, chair of the foundation, said, "Whether someone comes seeking food, parenting resources, educational support, workforce training, or guidance through a difficult season, our goal is simple: one place where people are welcomed, connected, and empowered.”The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry provides an established starting point for the project. Its reported monthly reach of around 3,000 individuals gives an indication of the demand for food assistance in the community and the role the new centre could play in extending that support.The planned expansion will place the pantry within a wider network of family and adult services. Residents will have access not only to food assistance but also to programmes intended to support education, financial understanding and employment prospects.The centre's effectiveness will depend on how these services are delivered and how well they meet local needs once the facility is operating. The announcement sets out the intended range of programmes, although it does not specify an opening date or provide a detailed timetable for their introduction.By combining food assistance with educational, parenting and employment services, the centre aims to address several practical challenges faced by families in one location.The project also extends the Davis-Tennon Foundation’s existing work in Rhode Island, with the new facility intended to provide a permanent base for its community programmes in Central Falls.
Article Summary: A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother. The actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a new family engagement centre in Central Falls, Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.

Article Title: Ohio approves easement purchases for 58 family farms covering 5,165 acres, as statewide protected farmland exceeds 111,000 acres while owners retain the right to farm their land
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

How the agricultural easement programme works

Which farms qualify for protection?

More than 111,000 acres now protected

Additional funding supports preservation efforts

As development puts pressure on agricultural land, keeping farms in production has become an important part of long-term land conservation. Ohio has taken another step in that direction, approving local sponsors to purchase agricultural easements on 58 family farms covering 5,165 acres across 36 counties. According to a report published by Ohio’s Country Journal on October 11, 2026, the approvals allow local sponsors to pursue easement purchases intended to protect the land from future non-agricultural development while farmers retain ownership and continue working their land. Ohio has more than 111,000 acres of permanently preserved farmland across 769 family farms in 62 counties, including land protected under related programmes.The latest approvals fall under Ohio’s Local Agricultural Easement Purchase Program (LAEPP), which uses public funding to help protect farmland from being converted to other uses. The programme allows local organisations to purchase agricultural easements from farmers who voluntarily agree to keep their land in agricultural production.These easements place a permanent restriction on how the land can be used.Farmers retain ownership and can continue working their fields, growing crops and operating their agricultural businesses. However, the land cannot simply be converted to non-agricultural development in the future. The programme is managed through local sponsors, including land trusts, county governments, townships and local soil and water conservation districts. These organisations work with landowners to submit applications and secure funding for eligible properties.Not every property automatically qualifies for an agricultural easement. Ohio has set eligibility requirements to ensure that the programme supports working farms and responsible land management. Generally, a farm must cover more than 40 acres or be adjacent to an already preserved farm. It must be actively farmed, participate in the Current Agricultural Use Value programme and demonstrate good stewardship of the land. Support from local government is also required, and the programme's eligibility rules restrict applications for farms located close to development. The easements are purchased through a competitive process, meaning eligible applications must be considered for available funding rather than receiving automatic approval.For farmers, the arrangement offers a way to receive compensation for agreeing to preserve their land permanently. Owners can use the proceeds as they choose, although some reinvest the money in their farming operations. This can help them fund improvements, support ongoing agricultural work or strengthen their businesses without giving up ownership of their property.The latest approvals build on two decades of farmland preservation efforts in Ohio. Between 2002 and 2025, the state preserved 100,954 acres through easements covering 689 family farms across 54 counties. When farmland protected under related programmes is included, Ohio's total has now crossed 111,000 acres. The preserved land spans 769 family farms across 62 counties, reflecting the programme's reach beyond the latest 58 farms.The newly approved easements cover properties in 36 counties, including Auglaize, Delaware, Fairfield, Greene, Miami, Montgomery, Ross, Union, Warren and Wood. The approvals therefore extend across a broad part of the state rather than concentrating preservation efforts in a single agricultural region.Federal funding has also helped Ohio expand its farmland protection work. In 2026, the Ohio Department of Agriculture secured an additional $2.4 million in federal matching funds through the US Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service and its Agricultural Conservation Easement Program (ACEP), Agricultural Land Easements (ALE) component. The additional funding supports efforts to preserve more farmland through agricultural easement purchases. Combined with funding from the Clean Ohio Conservation Fund, it supports the purchase of easements from landowners willing to enter the programme.The Clean Ohio Conservation Fund was approved by voters in 2008 and provides funding for conservation initiatives, including farmland preservation. The state is also preparing for the next round of applications. The certification period for local sponsors seeking to participate in the 2027 programme remains open through October 23, 2026. Eligible counties, townships, cities, soil and water conservation districts and land trusts can apply to become sponsors and receive an allocation of funds for purchasing agricultural easements.Ohio's latest approvals reflect a continuing effort to keep productive farmland in agricultural use as development pressures grow. By compensating willing owners while allowing them to continue farming, the programme aims to protect the state's agricultural base for future generations without requiring farmers to sell their land outright.
Article Summary: Ohio has approved local sponsors to purchase agricultural easements on 58 family farms covering 5,165 acres across 36 counties. The latest approvals build on two decades of farmland preservation efforts in Ohio. The state has more than 111,000 acres of permanently preserved farmland across 769 family farms in 62 counties, including land protected under related programmes.

Article Title: In 2018, Kevin Durant pledged $10 million over 10 years to create a college-access center in his Maryland hometown; today it serves 200+ students a year and reports a 96% four-year college acceptance
Article Text:
Kevin Durant/Image: Getty Images

A decade-long programme supporting students

What the college acceptance rate shows

Who is Kevin Durant?

NBA star Kevin Durant’s $10 million commitment to college access in his Maryland hometown is now supporting more than 200 students annually, with the education centre established through the initiative reporting a four-year college acceptance rate above 96%.Durant announced the 10-year pledge in 2018 through the Kevin Durant Charity Foundation, partnering with College Track to bring its college preparation and completion programme to Prince George’s County. The Durant Center opened in January 2019, giving students from underserved communities access to academic guidance and other resources intended to help them enter and graduate from university.The center, based in the community where Durant grew up, now serves students from partner schools including Suitland, Potomac and Charles Herbert Flowers high schools. According to College Track, 89% of its scholars at the Durant Center are first-generation college students, while 86% come from under-resourced backgrounds.College Track’s model begins in ninth grade and continues through college. Rather than focusing only on university applications, the programme aims to address academic, financial and social-emotional barriers that can prevent students from completing a degree.The Durant Center was established as the first College Track location on the East Coast. Its inaugural cohort included students from Suitland High School, near the neighbourhood where Durant grew up. The programme was designed to help participants navigate the transition from secondary school to higher education and remain supported through graduation.“This is the realisation of a dream of mine,” Durant said when announcing the commitment in 2018. “To come back home and positively impact the lives of kids – who share the ambitions I’ve always had – with world-class educational opportunities and resources that can completely change the game in our community for generations to come.”The initiative reflected Durant’s decision to direct part of his philanthropic work towards education in the area where he was raised. His foundation had previously supported youth athletics, basketball court construction and organisations working with young people experiencing homelessness.College Track reports that the Durant Center’s four-year college acceptance rate is above 96%. The figure indicates how many participating students receive offers from four-year institutions, rather than how many ultimately enrol or complete their degrees. The distinction matters because admission is only one stage of the college journey.The organisation’s wider programme is built around that longer process. Students receive support from high school through college, to help them manage academic requirements, financial pressures and other challenges that can affect degree completion.Kevin Durant is an American professional basketball player for the Houston Rockets and is widely regarded as one of the NBA’s greatest scorers. He has won two NBA championships, been named the league’s Most Valuable Player and received two NBA Finals MVP awards.Durant has also been selected as an NBA All-Star 16 times and won four Olympic gold medals representing the United States.
Article Summary: Durant announced the 10-year pledge in 2018 through the Kevin Durant Charity Foundation. The Durant Center opened in January 2019, giving students from underserved communities access to academic guidance and other resources. College Track’s model begins in ninth grade and continues through college.

Article Title: A Michigan couple bought land at a 2015 tax sale and claimed a 50-foot strip lost through a 1965 deed error; after two surveys put it with their neighbour, an appeals court ruled against them
Article Text:
The couple believed that a mistake made in a 1965 tax sale deed had changed the description of their property's boundary (AI image)

How a 1965 deed became the centre of the dispute

Disagreement escalated after locks were changed

What evidence did the couple present?

Michigan appeals court ruled against the couple

A couple in Michigan, United States, has lost a legal battle over a 50-foot-wide strip of land that they claimed belonged to their property because of an error in a deed dating back to 1965. Max W. Firman III and Dawn M. Kasner, who purchased their land at a tax sale in 2015, argued that the disputed strip had been used by previous owners of their property for decades. However, the Michigan Court of Appeals ruled against them on Friday, finding that they had not provided enough evidence to establish ownership.According to court documents, the dispute involved neighbouring properties in Rose Township, Ogemaw County. Firman and Kasner bought their parcel in 2015, while their neighbour, Antonio Santos, purchased the surrounding property in 2021. The disagreement began when Santos challenged the couple's claim over the strip of land, which also contained a structure.The couple believed that a mistake made in a 1965 tax sale deed had changed the description of their property's boundary. They relied on an earlier deed from 1955, which referred to a boundary measurement of 400 feet.However, the 1965 deed used 450 feet, and that description continued to appear in subsequent property records.The difference of 50 feet became the centre of the dispute. Although the couple claimed that the land and the structure on it had been used by previous owners of their property, two surveys commissioned by Santos placed the disputed area within his property. The disagreement eventually reached the courts, where the couple sought legal recognition of their ownership.The couple argued that the change in the property description in 1965 was an error that had remained uncorrected for decades. They maintained that the disputed strip should have been included with the land they purchased in 2015.They also claimed that previous owners had built, maintained and used the structure located on the disputed land. According to their case, they continued using the area after purchasing the property and believed that taxes had been paid on it by them and earlier owners.Santos disputed these claims. After buying the surrounding property in 2021, he commissioned two surveys, both of which showed that the 50-foot strip belonged to his property.He also submitted a photograph of the structure taken before the 2015 tax sale. A sign on the building read "NOT IN TAX SALE". Santos said his immediate predecessor had placed the sign there because photographs used in the tax sale listing had created the impression that the disputed area was included in the property being sold.The dispute became more serious after Santos purchased his property. Both sides accused each other of entering the disputed area without permission.In 2023, the local sheriff was contacted after Santos allegedly changed the locks on the structure and demolished some interior walls. The sheriff told the couple that the ownership dispute would have to be settled in court.Firman and Kasner filed a lawsuit in February 2024, seeking to establish ownership of the disputed land and raising a trespass claim. Santos responded with counterclaims, including trespass and nuisance.The trial court subsequently ruled in Santos's favour, finding that the couple's original claim was barred by Michigan's 15-year limitation period. The couple then amended their complaint, arguing that they and previous owners had acquired ownership through adverse possession or acquiescence.To support their case, the couple submitted a 1982 deed and a 2013 affidavit concerning earlier owners of their property.The 1982 deed referred to land possessed by the previous owners for more than 15 years "in this vicinity". The couple argued that this showed the earlier owners had already acquired rights over the disputed area.The 2013 affidavit also referred to an adverse possession claim by a previous owner, Vianne Samuels, concerning property interests not clearly established in the recorded ownership documents.Adverse possession is a legal principle under which someone may acquire ownership of land through possession that meets specific legal requirements over a prescribed period. In Michigan, the relevant period is 15 years.However, the appeals court found that neither document identified the disputed 50-foot strip. Both also continued to use the same property description found in the 1965 deed.The couple relied on tax records and the existence of the structure as further evidence. But the court found that these records did not establish who had built or used the structure, when it was built, or whether the disputed land had been openly and continuously possessed for the required period.The appeals court also considered the couple's argument of acquiescence, under which neighbouring owners may establish a property boundary by treating it as the accepted boundary for 15 years.The judges found insufficient evidence that previous owners of the neighbouring properties had accepted the boundary claimed by the couple. The sign stating "NOT IN TAX SALE" also indicated that Santos's immediate predecessor had not accepted their claimed boundary.In its October 9 ruling, the Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the trial court's decision dismissing the couple's amended complaint.However, the case has not ended entirely. The appeals court sent it back to the trial court for further proceedings concerning Santos's outstanding counterclaims, which were not decided in the appeal.
Article Summary: Max W. Firman III and Dawn M. Kasner argued that the disputed strip had been used by previous owners of their property for decades. The Michigan Court of Appeals ruled against them on Friday, finding that they had not provided enough evidence to establish ownership.

Article Title: In 1992, Tyler Perry put his $12,000 savings into a failed Atlanta play and later spent months living in a car; decades later his $750,000 gift helped pay back taxes for 300+ seniors and freeze taxes
Article Text:
Tyler Perry/Image: AP

How the donation will help Atlanta seniors

From a failed play to a billion-dollar fortune

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of Tyler Perry’s career impresses you the most? His success in film and television His philanthropic efforts His journey from hardship to success 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Tyler Perry, who once spent three months living in his car after losing $12,000 on a failed theatre production, has donated $750,000 to help low-income senior citizens in Atlanta pay property taxes and remain in their homes.Perry is an American filmmaker, actor, director, producer and writer, best known for creating the Madea character and building a career across theatre, film and television.He started out writing and performing stage plays in the 1990s before expanding into screen productions. His work includes more than 1,200 television episodes, 22 feature films and numerous stage plays.Perry founded Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta, where he continues to produce film and television content. According to Forbes, his fortune is estimated at $1.4.The contribution will cover outstanding property taxes for more than 300 low-income seniors and help another 100 avoid future increases through a pilot programme.Rising property taxes have put pressure on older residents living on fixed incomes, making it harder for some to remain in homes they have occupied for years. Perry’s donation will cover outstanding city, county and school property taxes, with the funds administered by Invest Atlanta Partnership, the nonprofit arm of the city’s economic development authority.The $750,000 contribution has two main purposes. The first is to clear overdue property taxes for more than 300 low-income senior residents in Atlanta. The assistance will cover taxes owed to the city, county and school authorities.The second part will support a pilot programme for 100 low-income seniors, using funds to cover the difference between their current property taxes and any increases. The aim is to help them manage rising costs and remain in their homes.“Atlanta’s growth and prosperity should not come at the expense of our legacy residents, many of whom have been priced out of their homes in previous years,” Mayor Dickens said.“Tyler Perry has been engaged in our ongoing conversations around legacy resident retention, and he told me he wanted to do something to support these efforts. Thanks to his generosity, more Atlantans will be able to remain in the communities they built.”Perry began his career in live theatre in the 1990s. He put $12,000 of his savings into producing I Know I’ve Been Changed, a play about survivors of child abuse, at a community theatre in Atlanta.The production initially failed to attract a large enough paying audience to cover his expenses. Perry struggled to pay rent and spent three months living in his car on and off while revising the show and trying to build an audience. He handled several aspects of the production himself, including designing the set, preparing programmes, hanging lights and selling snacks during intermissions.He continued touring his plays, gradually building a following before moving into film and television. His Madea franchise has grossed more than $660 million, as per the Forbes.Perry’s business model has also centred on retaining ownership of his work. In 2019, he opened Tyler Perry Studios, a 330-acre production complex in Atlanta. That year, he also struck a deal with Viacom that gave him a 25% stake in streaming service BET+.
Article Summary: Perry is an American filmmaker, actor, director, producer and writer. He is best known for creating the Madea character and building a career across theatre, film and television. The contribution will cover outstanding property taxes for more than 300 low-income seniors and help another 100 avoid future increases.

Article Title: Beyoncé's beauty brand is expanding its scholarship fund to the UK; 10 schools will receive $250,000 to train the next generation of hair professionals
Article Text:
Beyoncé’s Cécred scholarship fund expands to 10 schools with its first UK partnerships

How the fund supports students entering the hair industry

Representational Image

The programme began with a $500,000 investment in 2024

Beyoncé’s fund supported 37 salon owners and 46 students in 2025

Cécred’s beauty business and BeyGOOD’s charitable work

Beyoncé’s haircare business is extending its support for aspiring hair professionals beyond the United States, bringing its scholarship programme to the United Kingdom for the first time. Reportedly, the Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund has committed $250,000 to cosmetology and barbering education in 2026, with 10 schools set to receive $25,000 each. The funding is intended to help students cover tuition and other education-related costs as they prepare for careers in the beauty industry. The latest round doubles the number of participating schools from the previous five, building on a programme that has supported both students and salon owners since 2024.The Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund is increasing the number of educational institutions involved in its scholarship programme from five to 10 in 2026. The new intake also extends beyond the United States, with schools in the United Kingdom becoming part of the initiative for the first time since its launch in 2024.The fund has allocated $250,000 to this year's education programme. Each of the 10 selected institutions will receive $25,000 to support students studying cosmetology and barbering.The money is intended to help cover tuition and other education-related expenses, giving participating schools funding to direct towards students preparing for careers in the hair industry.The expansion builds on a programme that has previously operated in several US markets. Its move into the UK gives the fund an international presence, although the published announcement does not identify the 10 participating schools individually.The scholarship programme is part of a broader effort to support the people who work in salons and barbershops, including those still completing their training. Students need practical experience alongside their classroom education, and the costs associated with professional courses can include supplies and other materials required to develop technical skills.By directing funding through partner institutions, the Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund can contribute towards these expenses without limiting its support to established professionals. The 2026 allocation is dedicated to education, rather than being divided between students and existing business owners as it was during the fund's first year.Tina Knowles, chair of the BeyGOOD Foundation's board and vice chairwoman at Cécred described, “We strive to uplift the professional hair industry and grow the salon community, while giving students and salon owners the tools they need to progress it forward.”When the Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund launched in 2024, it committed $500,000 to supporting salon professionals and students. The initial programme covered five US states: California, Georgia, Illinois, New Jersey and Texas.Education received half of that first investment, amounting to $250,000. Twenty-five cosmetology students at five partner schools were awarded scholarships worth $10,000 each. The remaining $250,000 went to 25 salon and barbershop owners, who also received $10,000 apiece to help maintain or develop their businesses.That first round established the fund's two main areas of support. It addressed the training costs faced by people entering the profession while also offering financial assistance to those already running businesses in the sector.The fund widened its reach across the United States in 2025, maintaining its total investment at $500,000. Its support for established businesses grew, with $370,000 distributed among 37 salon and barbershop owners in grants of $10,000 each.Those recipients also had access to business development assistance, mentoring and other resources through a partnership with the National Minority Supplier Development Council (NMSDC). The arrangement extended the programme beyond direct grants by connecting owners with support intended to help them manage and develop their businesses.Students continued to receive funding that year, although the education allocation was smaller than in the inaugural round. A total of $130,000 was set aside for scholarships awarded to 46 cosmetology and barbering students.The 2026 programme takes a different approach. Rather than repeating the previous year's split between business grants and student scholarships, the announced $250,000 investment is focused on education. Doubling the number of participating schools and adding the UK gives the latest round a wider institutional reach, even as its total funding is lower than the $500,000 commitments made in each of the two preceding years.Cécred is Beyoncé's haircare brand, while BeyGOOD is the philanthropic organisation associated with the singer. Their joint fund brings the two together around an industry in which training, technical knowledge and small-business ownership are closely linked.Salon professionals often build their careers through formal education followed by practical work, and some eventually establish businesses of their own. The fund's earlier rounds reflected both stages, with scholarships for students and grants for salon and barbershop owners. Its latest allocation places greater emphasis on the training stage, with schools serving as the route through which financial assistance will reach students.For 2026, the immediate commitment is clear: 10 institutions will receive $25,000 each, bringing the total education investment to $250,000. The inclusion of UK schools extends the programme beyond its original American base. Which institutions will take part, and how the individual schools will distribute the funding, remain details to be confirmed in the published announcement.
Article Summary: The Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund has committed $250,000 to cosmetology and barbering education in 2026. The funding is intended to help students cover tuition and other education-related costs as they prepare for careers in the beauty industry. The expansion builds on a programme that has previously operated in several US markets.

Article Title: Melinda French Gates and her daughters backed a $70 million fund; 22 organisations received money to tackle women's health and violence
Article Text:
How Melinda French Gates and her daughters backed the $70 million fund

Three areas the fund aims to address

Maternal health

Sexual and reproductive health and rights

Preventing gender-based violence

Why the grants are unrestricted

Ujamaa Africa receives $3 million

Who else is backing the initiative?

Why women's health and safety are a priority

Melinda French Gates and her daughters, Jennifer Gates Nassar and Phoebe Gates, joined other philanthropists in backing a $70 million initiative to improve women's health and address gender-based violence. Launched in September 2025, the Women's Health Co-Lab brought together donors through ICONIQ Impact and Co-Impact to support 22 organisations working on maternal healthcare, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and violence prevention.
